passages.title: Forty Minutes and One Pan
passages.passage:
The rules of the Riverside Youth Cooking Cup are simple, and that is exactly what makes it hard. Each team of two receives the same basket of ingredients, one pan, one small stove and forty minutes. Nobody knows what is in the basket until a bell rings. Last Saturday, in the town hall, twelve teams opened their baskets to find a fish, three eggs, a bunch of spring onions, half a lemon and a bag of rice.

Fourteen-year-old Linh and her partner Bao had been practising for weeks, but not in the way most people expected. "We didn't learn recipes," Linh explains. "We learned to plan. In the first two minutes we decide who does what, and we don't change the plan even if something goes wrong." While Bao boiled the rice, Linh cleaned the fish and cut the onions. Their fish rice with lemon and egg was ready with three minutes to spare.

Other teams were less fortunate. One pair spent so long arguing about what to cook that their rice was still hard when the final bell rang. Another team produced a dish the judges described as "beautiful but cold", because they had plated it too early. The head judge, a chef named Mr Duc, said afterwards that the contest was never really about cooking. "I'm watching how they work under pressure," he said. "A calm team with a plain dish will beat a talented team in chaos every time."

Linh and Bao finished second. The winners, two boys from a school across the river, made a fish soup that Mr Duc called "the only dish I wanted a second bowl of". Linh says she is not disappointed. "We did what we planned to do," she says. "Next year we'll plan something braver." The organisers have already announced that next year's basket will contain one ingredient that most of the contestants will never have cooked before.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why Linh and Bao failed to win the Riverside Youth Cooking Cup
The history of cooking competitions held in the town hall
How to cook fish rice with lemon and egg in under forty minutes
A cooking contest and what the judges were really looking for
questions.explanation: The passage describes the contest and returns to the same idea: the judges cared about planning and calm under pressure, not just food. The recipe and the second place are details.

questions.q: How did Linh and Bao prepare for the competition?
options: They memorised a large number of recipes.
They practised cooking fish soup every weekend.
They practised dividing the work and sticking to a plan.
They asked Mr Duc for advice about the basket.
questions.explanation: Linh says, "We didn't learn recipes. We learned to plan," and that they decide who does what and do not change the plan. Fish soup was the winners' dish, not theirs.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the team whose dish was "beautiful but cold"?
options: They used more than one pan.
They finished cooking too long before the judges tasted it.
They forgot to turn on their stove.
They spent most of the time arguing.
questions.explanation: The passage says they had "plated it too early", so the food cooled before the judges tasted it. The arguing team is a different pair mentioned in the same paragraph.

questions.q: The word "chaos" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
options: complete disorder
a small kitchen
great skill
silence
questions.explanation: Mr Duc contrasts "a calm team" with "a talented team in chaos". The opposite of calm here is disorder or confusion.

questions.q: In paragraph 1, "that" in "that is exactly what makes it hard" refers to
options: the bell
the basket of ingredients
the town hall
the fact that the rules are simple
questions.explanation: The sentence says the rules are simple, and "that" (the simplicity) is what makes the contest hard.

questions.q: Linh and Bao's dish was finished before the time ran out.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage says their dish "was ready with three minutes to spare", so it was finished before the forty minutes ended.

questions.q: Mr Duc tasted every dish twice.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: He said the winners' soup was the only dish he "wanted a second bowl of", but the passage never says how many times he actually tasted any dish.

passages.title: Where the Town Wakes Up
passages.passage:
If you want to know what a town is really like, do not visit its museum. Go to its street market at six in the morning. In Tan An, a small town in the south, the market fills three streets around an old banyan tree, and by the time most people are awake, half of the day's business is already done.

The market has no roof and no fixed stalls. Each seller arrives with a bamboo basket, a plastic sheet or, at most, a small cart, and takes the same spot every day. Mrs Hai, who has sold bananas under the banyan tree for twenty-two years, says the sellers have their own quiet system. "Nobody has written it down," she says, "but everyone knows whose place is whose. If a new person sits in my spot, the others will explain it to them before I even arrive."

Prices here are rarely fixed. A customer asks, the seller answers, and the real price is somewhere in between. Visitors from the city sometimes find this tiring, but regular customers say it is the best part of the morning. "It isn't really about saving money," says Mr Thanh, a retired teacher who shops there daily. "You ask about her grandson, she asks about your knee, and then you agree on a price. It's how we stay friends."

The market is not without problems. Motorbikes squeeze between the baskets, and on rainy days the streets turn to mud. Two years ago, the town council proposed moving all the sellers into a new covered building on the edge of town. The plan was dropped after almost every seller refused to go. "A market is not a building," Mrs Hai said at the meeting. "It's the people who come to it, and they won't walk that far."

For now, the banyan tree stays, and so do the baskets beneath it. By nine o'clock the streets are almost empty again, swept clean, as if the market had never been there at all.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the passage?
options: A guide to the cheapest fruit in Tan An
An argument for moving markets into modern buildings
A description of a street market and why people value it
The life story of a banana seller
questions.explanation: The passage describes how the market works, how people bargain and why sellers refused to move. Mrs Hai is one example, not the whole subject.

questions.q: How do sellers know where to set up each day?
options: The first seller to arrive chooses the best place.
Mrs Hai decides where the new sellers should sit.
The town council gives each seller a written permit.
There is an unwritten agreement that everyone understands.
questions.explanation: Mrs Hai says "Nobody has written it down, but everyone knows whose place is whose." It is a shared understanding, not a permit or a first-come rule.

questions.q: What does Mr Thanh suggest about bargaining?
options: It is a social habit that keeps people connected.
It is something only city visitors enjoy.
It should be replaced by fixed prices.
It is mainly a way to get the lowest price.
questions.explanation: He says "It isn't really about saving money" and describes asking about family and health before agreeing a price. For him, bargaining is about friendship.

questions.q: The word "proposed" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to
options: refused
suggested
finished
forgot
questions.explanation: The council "proposed moving all the sellers" and the plan was later dropped, so the council put forward or suggested the idea rather than carrying it out.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention motorbikes and rainy days?
options: To prove that the new building was a better idea
To describe the town's main tourist attraction
To show that the market has real disadvantages
To explain why the market closes by nine o'clock
questions.explanation: The paragraph begins "The market is not without problems," and the motorbikes and mud are examples of those problems. The writer does not say the building was better.

questions.q: The covered building was built on the edge of town but the sellers refused to use it.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The building was only proposed, and "the plan was dropped". The passage does not say it was ever built.

questions.q: Mrs Hai has sold bananas at the market for more than twenty years.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage says she has sold bananas under the banyan tree "for twenty-two years", which is more than twenty.

passages.title: Ten Minutes Before Breakfast
passages.passage:
When Khanh, aged thirteen, asked for a guitar, his parents agreed on one condition: he had to keep playing for a year. He said yes without thinking. Three weeks later, his fingertips hurt, the strings buzzed whenever he touched them, and the guitar was leaning in a corner of his bedroom, gathering dust.

What changed things was not a better teacher or a more expensive instrument. It was a suggestion from his uncle, who had played in a band when he was young. "Don't try to practise for an hour," his uncle said. "You'll never find an hour. Play for ten minutes before breakfast, every single day, and don't miss one." Khanh thought ten minutes was too short to be useful, but he agreed to try.

The first month was boring. He played the same three chords again and again while his rice was getting cold. But because the sessions were so short, he never had a reason to skip one. By the second month, the buzzing had stopped. By the third, he could change chords without looking at his fingers, and he began adding a fourth chord, then a fifth.

Music teachers say this pattern is common. Learners who practise a little every day usually improve faster than those who practise for a long time once a week, because the hands forget quickly. A short daily session also removes the biggest obstacle, which is simply starting. "The hardest note," one teacher told me, "is the first one."

Khanh has now played for fourteen months, longer than the year his parents asked for. He still practises before breakfast, though the sessions have grown to twenty minutes because he does not want to stop. Last week he played his first song in front of his class. He made two mistakes in the middle, and nobody noticed. "I used to think I wasn't musical," he says. "Now I think I just wasn't patient."

questions.q: What is the main message of the passage?
options: Expensive instruments make learning easier.
Short, regular practice is more effective than occasional long sessions.
Children should not be forced to learn music.
Learning the guitar always hurts your fingers at first.
questions.explanation: The uncle's advice, Khanh's progress and the teachers' view all support the same point: a little practice every day works better than a long session once a week.

questions.q: Why had Khanh stopped playing after three weeks?
options: Playing was painful and the sound was poor.
He was too busy with school to find an hour.
His parents took the guitar away.
His uncle told him to wait until he was older.
questions.explanation: The passage says his fingertips hurt and the strings buzzed, and the guitar was left in a corner. The hour problem is what the uncle warns about later, not why he stopped.

questions.q: Why did the short sessions help Khanh keep going?
options: Because he could play five chords by the end of the first week
Because ten minutes was too little time to feel any pain
Because his uncle checked on him every morning
Because it was hard to find an excuse to miss such a short session
questions.explanation: The passage says that "because the sessions were so short, he never had a reason to skip one". Nothing suggests his uncle checked on him.

questions.q: The word "obstacle" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to
options: a kind of chord
a long lesson
something that blocks progress
a musical instrument
questions.explanation: The sentence explains that the biggest obstacle "is simply starting", so the word means a difficulty or barrier that stops you from moving forward.

questions.q: In paragraph 4, "this pattern" refers to
options: the three chords Khanh played
improving steadily through short daily practice
the way rice gets cold during practice
the sound of strings buzzing
questions.explanation: "This pattern" points back to Khanh's experience in paragraph 3, where daily ten-minute sessions led to gradual improvement, and the teachers say this is common.

questions.q: Khanh's classmates noticed the mistakes in his song.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage says he made two mistakes "and nobody noticed".

questions.q: Khanh's uncle still plays in a band.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: We are told only that the uncle "had played in a band when he was young". Whether he plays now is not mentioned.

passages.title: The Paper Nobody Picked Up
passages.passage:
For years, the newspaper at Binh Minh Secondary School was printed four times a year, and for years it went straight from the printer to the recycling bin. It contained the head teacher's message, a list of exam results and a poem chosen by the literature department. Students walked past the pile by the front gate without looking at it.

That changed when a grade 9 student named Trang took over as editor. Her first decision was to ask a simple question in every class: "What would you actually read?" The answers surprised the teachers. Nobody wanted the exam results. Students wanted to know which food stall near the school was worth the walk, why the football pitch was closed for a month, and whether the rumour about a new uniform was true.

Trang's team of eight reporters set out to answer those questions. They interviewed the school cook, timed the queue at the canteen and tested every drink sold outside the gate. When the football pitch story revealed that the money for repairs had been delayed, the head teacher was not pleased at first. But she allowed the article to be printed, and the repairs were finished two weeks later.

The paper now comes out every month, and copies disappear within a day. It is still printed rather than posted online because, as Trang points out, phones are not allowed in class but a folded newspaper can be read under a desk. Teachers have accepted this with a smile.

Not everything has worked. A column of anonymous complaints had to be stopped after it turned into a place for arguments between classes. Trang says the team learned an important lesson from it. "A newspaper is not a wall for shouting," she says. "Every story needs a name on it, and someone willing to explain why they wrote it." She graduates next year and is already training the grade 8 student who will replace her.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How a school newspaper became popular by reporting what students cared about
Why exam results should not be published in school newspapers
The problems caused by a column of anonymous complaints
How the head teacher repaired the school football pitch
questions.explanation: The whole passage traces the paper from being ignored to being read within a day, because Trang asked what students would actually read. The complaints column and the pitch are details.

questions.q: What was Trang's first action as editor?
options: She replaced the old team of reporters.
She asked students in every class what they would read.
She moved the newspaper online.
She wrote an article about the football pitch.
questions.explanation: The passage states that "her first decision was to ask a simple question in every class". The pitch article came later, and the paper is still printed, not online.

questions.q: What does the passage suggest about the football pitch article?
options: It caused arguments between classes.
It was never printed because the head teacher stopped it.
It helped speed up the repairs to the pitch.
It was written by the head teacher herself.
questions.explanation: The head teacher allowed the article, and "the repairs were finished two weeks later", which suggests the story pushed the work forward. The arguments came from the complaints column.

questions.q: The word "anonymous" in paragraph 5 is closest in meaning to
options: printed in colour
very long
written in a foreign language
without the writer's name
questions.explanation: The column was stopped and Trang concludes that "every story needs a name on it", so anonymous means the writers' names were not given.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention that phones are not allowed in class?
options: To explain why the paper is printed instead of published online
To show that students prefer reading on screens
To suggest that teachers dislike the newspaper
To criticise the school's strict rules
questions.explanation: The sentence directly explains the decision to print: a phone cannot be used in class, but a folded paper can be read under a desk.

questions.q: The newspaper is now published more often than it used to be.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: It was printed four times a year before, and "now comes out every month", which is more frequent.
